Positions within Farm Labor Contractors vary widely (providing seasonal workers for orchards and greenhouses, contract workers for livestock and dairy operations, work crews for forestry and nurseries, or staffing services specializing in dispatch and payroll settlement). Crops, seasons, regions, workforce size, and responsibility for transportation and accommodation also differ. Before comparing positions, check workers and work types covered, transportation and accommodation duties, wage and working time settlement definitions, and local licensing and registration requirements for farm labor contractors.

Test this through a paper exercise: given entirely fictional staffing needs (crops and work types, season length, worker numbers, worksites, accommodation and transportation conditions, wage and working time settlement arrangements, and assumed local minimum wage and overtime rules) and compliance conditions, write the recruitment and eligibility verification sequence, workforce and working time information to record, wage calculation and payment processes, accommodation and transportation safety points, and situations requiring work to stop and the issue to be reported.

Signals worth considering further: willingness to maintain accurate wages, working time, and records under contracts and regulations, communicate clearly with workers speaking different languages during seasonal peaks, and take responsibility for accommodation and transportation safety. Signals requiring caution: treating workers and wage records as matters that can be handled arbitrarily, compromising wages or transportation safety, or treating licenses and registration as things that can be obtained afterward.
This card is a career exploration reference; it does not constitute a hiring decision, ability score, or legal or compliance conclusion.

First assess whether you are willing to perform recruitment, worker dispatch, payroll settlement, and worksite condition organization and compliance work over the long term, and accept seasonal work and outdoor inspections; test this through this page's paper exercise and seven-day tasks.

Farm Labor Contractors' daily work centers on an agricultural staffing organization and compliance cycle: coordinate farm owners' staffing needs, confirm crops and working seasons, and recruit and hire seasonal or temporary agricultural workers; verify identity and work eligibility materials, arrange and direct workers to appropriate worksites, and provide tools; hire crew leaders to manage workers directly on site; record working time and calculate and pay wages under contracts and local wage rules; provide workers with food, drinking water, and field sanitation facilities, and arrange safe and compliant accommodation and transportation when responsible for them; also retain staffing, wage, and safety records and handle registration, reporting, and inspections.
U.S. O*NET-SOC 13-1074.00, Farm Labor Contractors: recruit and hire seasonal or temporary agricultural workers; may provide workers with transportation, accommodation, and meals.

Work context | Farm Labor Contractors work between employers, workers, and administrative authorities, completing a staffing cycle through confirming needs, recruiting and hiring, dispatch and transportation, on-site supervision, working time records, and payroll settlement.
Work locations | Farms, orchards, greenhouses, ranches, nurseries, and forestry worksites, staffing service offices, and worker accommodation; travel between multiple worksites is required.
Working conditions | Primarily outdoor and seasonal work, requiring prolonged movement between fields and operating sites, with exposure to sun, dust, and agricultural machinery environments; working hours extend considerably during staffing peaks, and most practitioners work more than 40 hours per week.
Main subjects | Agricultural workers and crews, positions and seasons, working time and wage records, tools and transportation vehicles, accommodation and living facilities, employment contracts, and compliance documents.
Collaboration | Work with farm owners and managers, on-site crew leaders, payroll and bookkeeping staff, transportation and accommodation providers, and labor and safety authorities.
Tools and materials | Staffing and wage record forms, bookkeeping and office software (such as accounting, spreadsheet, and database software), communication tools, transportation vehicles and safety checklists, employment contracts, and regulatory texts.

Documentation requirements | Workforce and working time, wage calculation and payment, accommodation and transportation arrangements, safety inspections, and registration certificates must leave an auditable trail and be traceable as required.

entries.answer: Recruit and hire seasonal or temporary agricultural workers for farm owners: confirm staffing needs and seasons, recruit and hire workers and verify identity and work eligibility materials; arrange and direct workers to appropriate worksites and provide tools; record working time and pay wages under contracts and local wage rules; provide workers with food, drinking water, and field sanitation facilities, and ensure safe and compliant accommodation and transportation when responsible for them; hire crew leaders to manage workers directly on site, and fulfill registration, documentation, and reporting duties under competent authorities' requirements.
entries.question: What do Farm Labor Contractors mainly do?

entries.answer: The subjects of responsibility differ: this occupation organizes, dispatches, and settles others' staffing for third-party farm owners and carries compliance responsibility for wage records, accommodation, and transportation; farm owners and agricultural managers run their own farms and decide production; agricultural frontline supervisors manage only a single farm's internal crew; general and operations managers concern overall organizational operations; human resources specialists concern recruitment and personnel across general industries, without responsibility for agricultural staffing field conditions or transportation and accommodation.

entries.answer: O*NET places this occupation in Job Zone 1–2 (little to some preparation), SVP below 6.0. In the education survey, approximately 49% reported requiring a high school diploma, 23% less than high school, and 12% a bachelor's degree. BLS lists no formal educational credential and short-term on-the-job training as typical entry preparation, commonly requiring less than 5 years of related experience. In the United States, federal law requires farm labor contractors to register with the U.S. Department of Labor, with additional conditions for accommodation, transportation, or driving. entries.answer: A more accurate judgment is that tools will assist some tasks and the occupation overall will primarily experience augmentation and structural adjustment. The ILO's 2023 study shows large differences in task exposure between occupations, and technical feasibility does not mean employer adoption. Wage calculation and payment, identity and work eligibility verification, and transportation and accommodation safety inspections require on-site verification and legal responsibility, so the conclusion is that working methods will change rather than the occupation being replaced entirely.
entries.question: Will AI replace this occupation?

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of workers' wage distribution within the same statistical period, not starting pay. This occupation is small and percentile estimates have greater uncertainty; employment arrangements (hourly, piece-rate, or seasonal lump-sum), region and crop seasons, and responsibility for transportation and accommodation all affect actual income.

entries.answer: Yes, but independently conducting contracting business has additional conditions. Typical U.S. entry preparation for this occupation is no formal educational credential and short-term on-the-job training, and some positions accept experience to address gaps. However, lawful farm labor contracting operations in the United States require registration with the U.S. Department of Labor, with additional conditions for accommodation, transportation, or driving. Feasibility depends on target employer, local regulations, and competent authorities' requirements; this page does not replace original regulations.
